title: The end of the road
theme: The one whose charioteer is understanding and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the far end of the road — the highest place of Viṣṇu.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «विवेकबुद्धिसारथिः», whose charioteer is the discerning intellect

words.role: sets this case against the one in 1.3.7

words.context: Śaṅkara: «प्रगृहीतमनाः समाहितचित्तः सन्», one whose mind is held, whose thought is collected

words.role: subject of āpnoti, picking up yaḥ

words.context: Śaṅkara: «संसारगतेः», of the course of saṃsāra

sandhi.type: iḥ before a voiced sound; aḥ before t
sandhi.rule: The visarga after i becomes r before the voiced y (it stands for an original s, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः)); the visarga of yaḥ becomes s before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).
The final n of the nominative °vān meets the initial n of naraḥ and both are written; nothing changes.
saḥ before a short a: the visarga becomes u and a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), and the initial a is absorbed, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति) (written with avagraha).
A final t becomes d before the voiced v, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
A final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).

samasa.vigraha: मनः एव प्रग्रहः, सः अस्य अस्ति

morphology.note: The possessive suffix -vat (nominative masculine -vān) is added to the compound manaḥ-pragraha, ‘mind as reins’; the chariot image of 1.3.3 is kept: the mind is the reins (pragraha).
Genitive singular of adhvan, ‘road, journey’, an n-stem; the strong stem adhvān- appears in the nominative.

translation.literal: But the man who has understanding as charioteer, who has the mind as reins — he reaches the far end of the road; that [is] the highest step of Viṣṇu.
translation.readable: But the one whose charioteer is understanding, who holds the reins of the mind, reaches the end of the road: that is the highest place of Viṣṇu.

anvaya: यः तु नरः विज्ञानसारथिः मनःप्रग्रहवान् [भवति], सः अध्वनः पारम् आप्नोति; तत् विष्णोः परमम् पदम् [अस्ति] ।
syntax: A relative sentence (yaḥ tu … naraḥ, with two bahuvrīhi-type predicates) is picked up by saḥ, the subject of āpnoti. The last quarter is a nominal sentence in apposition: tat, ‘that’ — the far end of the road — is the highest step of Viṣṇu.

ambiguities.note: 1.3.7–8 spoke of ‘that step’ (tat padam) without naming it; this verse names it, and 1.3.10–11 will say what lies beyond the senses, step by step, up to the Person. Śaṅkara: «परमं प्रकृष्टं पदं स्थानम् , सतत्त्वमित्येतत्» — the highest place, that is, the reality itself. Raṅgarāmānuja: «संसाराध्वपारभूतं परमात्मस्वरूपं», the supreme Self, which is the far end of the road of saṃsāra.

Śaṅkara explains the name by its root sense ‘pervading’ and identifies it with Brahman, the supreme Self called Vāsudeva: «व्यापनशीलस्य ब्रह्मणः परमात्मनो वासुदेवाख्यस्य». The words tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam are also the opening of a Ṛgveda verse (1.22.20).

beginner: This verse finishes the picture of the chariot that began a few verses earlier. Your body is the chariot, your senses are the horses, your mind is the reins, your understanding is the driver, and you are the passenger. Now we hear where the chariot is going. A person whose driver is clear understanding, and who keeps a steady hand on the reins of the mind, comes to the end of the road. That end has a name: the highest place of Viṣṇu. Śaṅkara explains Viṣṇu as ‘the one who pervades everything’, that is, Brahman itself, so the end of the road is the reality behind everything. Raṅgarāmānuja says the end of the road is the supreme Self. The road is the long wandering of birth and death; its end is where the wandering stops.
analogy: A long journey by road is not finished by driving faster but by arriving: once the destination is reached, the driving is over.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It completes the contrast of 1.3.7–8: the person whose charioteer is understanding and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the far end of the road, and that end is named the highest step of Viṣṇu.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: the driver, the reins, and the place
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He opens with the question the verse answers: «किं तत्पदमित्याह». The charioteer is the discerning intellect, «विवेकबुद्धिसारथिः»; holding the mind's reins is having the mind collected, «प्रगृहीतमनाः समाहितचित्तः सन्». The road is the course of saṃsāra («संसारगतेः»), and reaching its end means release from all its bonds: «मुच्यते सर्वसंसारबन्धनैः». Viṣṇu is the pervading Brahman, the supreme Self called Vāsudeva, and his highest place is «स्थानम् , सतत्त्वमित्येतत्».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the end of the road is the supreme Self
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He too reads the verse as the answer to ‘what is that step?’ («किं तत् पदम् ? इत्याकाङ्क्षायां»): the one with sound understanding and mind «समीचीनविज्ञानमनश्शाली संसाराध्वपारभूतं परमात्मस्वरूपं प्राप्नोति इत्यर्थः» — reaches the nature of the supreme Self, the far end of the road of saṃsāra.

commentary.q: Why name the goal only here?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Verses 1.3.7 and 1.3.8 speak only of ‘that step’ (tat padam), reached or not reached. The answer comes in the closing quarter of this verse, in words that echo the Ṛgveda (1.22.20, tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam). The next two verses then explain what lies between the senses and that goal.

advaita.text: The highest place of Viṣṇu is the reality of the pervading Brahman, the supreme Self — «व्यापनशीलस्य ब्रह्मणः परमात्मनो वासुदेवाख्यस्य»; reaching it is release from the bonds of saṃsāra.

visistadvaita.text: The end of the road is the supreme Self itself, reached by the one whose understanding and mind are sound: «संसाराध्वपारभूतं परमात्मस्वरूपं प्राप्नोति».

schools.disagreement: Both read ‘the highest step of Viṣṇu’ as the supreme reality at the end of saṃsāra; they part, as elsewhere, on whether reaching it is knowing one's own identity with it (Śaṅkara) or attaining the supreme Self as distinct (Raṅgarāmānuja). Madhva's bhāṣya, in our source, has no comment on this verse: his comment after 1.3.11 concerns 1.3.10–11.

parallels.quote: तद् विष्णोः परमं पदं सदा पश्यन्ति सूरयः
parallels.note: The verse's last quarter repeats the opening words of this Ṛgveda verse: the highest step of Viṣṇu, which the seers always see.

parallels.quote: संयतैस्त्वध्वनः पारं तद्विष्णोः परमं पदमाप्नोति इति दर्शयित्वा
parallels.note: Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya reads 1.3.10–11 as the answer to this verse: having shown that one with the senses restrained reaches the highest step of Viṣṇu, the text says what that is.

contemporary.text: Much effort goes into steering well — attention, habits, discipline — and less into asking where the steering is meant to take us. The verse holds the two together: a steady hand on the reins, and a destination worth arriving at. Control without a goal is only motion. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: If your life were a journey by chariot, who would you say is driving most of the time — understanding, or the horses?
reflect.deeper: Why might the goal be named only after the description of the driver and the reins, and not before?
reflect.practice: At the start of a task, name in one sentence where it is meant to lead. At its end, check whether it did.

flags.note: ‘The highest step of Viṣṇu’: the reality of the pervading Brahman (Śaṅkara), or the supreme Self as the goal attained (Raṅgarāmānuja). Madhva's bhāṣya has no comment on the verse.
